# Hillradar AI

> Hillradar AI (https://hillradar.com) is a public-records research tool that tracks the stock trades US senators and representatives are legally required to disclose under the STOCK Act. It turns Periodic Transaction Reports into a searchable database with lawmaker profiles, company views, activity clusters and alerts. It is independent, non-partisan, not affiliated with the US Government, and provides no financial advice.

## Key facts
- Coverage: every disclosed congressional stock trade since 2014 (57,000+ filings, 350+ lawmakers, 9,000+ companies and assets), refreshed several times a day.
- Sources: official House Clerk and Senate eFD disclosure filings via open datasets, plus the official congress-legislators directory for names, parties, chambers, states and photos.
- Amounts are the ranges lawmakers report (e.g. $15,001–$50,000); the law allows up to 45 days to file after a trade and late filings are marked.
- Plans: Free (last 30 days of filings, profiles, 1 watchlist item). Pro: $497 per year (full history, AI Scanning of activity clusters with plain-English reasons, Investment Plan back-test and calculator, Telegram/WhatsApp/email alerts, unlimited watchlist, CSV export). 14-day refund on a first Pro payment.
- Audience: journalists, researchers, voters, compliance teams and self-directed investors who want the primary source.
- Contact: info@hillradar.com

## Blog
- [The STOCK Act, explained: what members of Congress must disclose, and when](https://hillradar.com/blog/what-is-the-stock-act/): What the 2012 STOCK Act requires US senators and representatives to disclose about their stock trades, the 45-day deadline, what a filing contains, and where the records are published.
- [How to read a congressional Periodic Transaction Report (PTR), field by field](https://hillradar.com/blog/how-to-read-a-periodic-transaction-report/): A line-by-line guide to a congressional stock trade filing: owner codes, asset names and tickers, transaction type, dates, amount ranges, and the traps that trip up first-time readers.
- [Congress stock trades by the numbers: 57,262 filings from 2014 to 2026](https://hillradar.com/blog/congress-stock-trades-by-the-numbers/): Every disclosed congressional transaction since 2014 in one data story: filings per year, buys versus sells, Republicans versus Democrats, House versus Senate, and the states that trade the most.
- [The 15 stocks traded by the most members of Congress](https://hillradar.com/blog/most-traded-stocks-by-members-of-congress/): Which companies appear in the most lawmakers' disclosures? Apple, Microsoft and Amazon lead a list of 15 stocks ranked by how many members of Congress have bought or sold them since 2014.
- [The 45-day rule: how late Congress really files its stock trades](https://hillradar.com/blog/congress-45-day-filing-rule-and-late-disclosures/): The STOCK Act gives lawmakers 45 days to disclose a trade. We measured the gap on 57,262 filings: the median is 27 days, but 14.6% are late and 5,548 arrived more than 90 days after the trade.
- [The most active stock traders in Congress, ranked by disclosed transactions](https://hillradar.com/blog/most-active-stock-traders-in-congress/): Ten members of Congress account for roughly a third of all 57,262 disclosed transactions since 2014. Here is the ranking, with buys, sells and active years, and what a high count does and does not mean.
- [Why congressional stock trades are reported as ranges, and how to use them anyway](https://hillradar.com/blog/why-congress-trade-amounts-are-ranges/): Lawmakers never disclose exact dollar amounts, only bands like $15,001–$50,000. Here are the bands, how 57,262 filings are distributed across them, and the honest way to estimate volume.
- [How to get alerts when a member of Congress files a stock trade](https://hillradar.com/blog/how-to-get-alerts-for-congress-stock-trades/): A step-by-step guide to being told the moment a congressional trade is disclosed: choosing who to follow, connecting Telegram, WhatsApp or email, and what an alert actually contains.
- [What is a congressional trading cluster, and how AI Scanning finds one](https://hillradar.com/blog/what-is-a-congressional-trading-cluster/): When several members of Congress file trades in the same company within a few weeks, that is a cluster. Here is how Hillradar AI detects and scores them, what the back-test shows, and the caveats that come with it.
- [House vs Senate: how congressional stock trade disclosures differ](https://hillradar.com/blog/house-vs-senate-stock-trade-disclosures/): The two chambers file under the same law but produce very different records: 46,096 House transactions against 11,166 in the Senate, different speeds, different owner patterns and different file formats.
